title: Null Object, Specification, and Choosing Behavioral Patterns
scopeHtml: Scope: Null Object, Specification, and a decision guide comparing behavioral patterns.

notes.title: Null Object: the idea
notes.html:
Null Object is a do-nothing implementation of an interface that you hand out instead of null. The caller never needs if (x != null); it just calls the method, and the null object does a harmless default (nothing, zero, empty list).

Why it matters: null checks scatter across the code, and one forgotten check is a NullPointerException in production. Tony Hoare called null his "billion dollar mistake".

+----------------+          +------------------+
| <<interface>>  |          | Client           |
| Logger         |<---------| uses Logger      |
| + log(msg)     |          +------------------+
+-------+--------+
        ^
  +-----+-------------+
  |                   |
FileLogger        NoOpLogger   (null object: log() does nothing)

Before:

class Service {
    private final Logger logger;            // may be null
    void run() {
        if (logger != null) logger.log("start");
        doWork();
        if (logger != null) logger.log("end");   // easy to forget one
    }
}

After:

interface Logger { void log(String msg); }
class ConsoleLogger implements Logger { public void log(String m) { System.out.println(m); } }
class NoOpLogger implements Logger { public void log(String m) { /* intentionally nothing */ } }

class Service {
    private final Logger logger;
    Service(Logger logger) { this.logger = logger; }   // never null
    void run() { logger.log("start"); doWork(); logger.log("end"); }
}
// new Service(new NoOpLogger()).run();

Kotlin variant. Kotlin has null safety in the type system, so many cases use ?. and ?: instead. A null object is still right when a behaviour (not just a value) should default to nothing:

interface Logger { fun log(msg: String) }
object NoOpLogger : Logger { override fun log(msg: String) {} }

class Service(private val logger: Logger = NoOpLogger) {
    fun run() { logger.log("start") }
}
// Value case: prefer emptyList() over null
fun loadTags(): List<String> = emptyList()

Real examples. Collections.emptyList(), Collections.emptyIterator(); java.util.Optional.empty() (a value-wrapper cousin); SLF4J NOPLogger; Android NoOp ImageLoader fakes, RecyclerView.ItemAnimator set to null vs a no-op, Handler.Callback; Mockito's default answers return empty values; Kotlin Unit; Glide RequestListener defaults; Android Log stripped by R8 in release (rules replace calls with no-ops).

Worked example. 12 call sites check logger != null. One teammate adds the 13th site and forgets: NPE only when logging is disabled (a rare config), caught after release. With NoOpLogger, logging is never null, 0 branches to forget, and unit tests can inject a recording logger.

Decision gravity. Easy to add, reversible. The hidden risk: a null object hides a missing dependency. If "no discount" is a legitimate rule, great; if "no payment gateway configured" silently succeeds, you have a worse bug than the NPE. Use it where doing nothing is the correct behaviour.

Everyday analogy. A blank placeholder name tag at a conference: a guest without a badge still gets one that reads "Guest", so nobody has to check for an empty hand.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Null Object where failure should be loud (payments, security).
  • Returning null from a method returning a collection; return empty.
  • Forgetting there can be one shared immutable instance (singleton); do not allocate a new one each time.

notes.title: When NOT to use Null Object
notes.html:
• Absence is meaningful and callers must react (user not found -> 404). Use Optional, a nullable type, or a sealed Result so the caller is forced to decide.
  • The default behaviour is not obvious or safe. A "NullPaymentProcessor" that returns success is dangerous.
  • Only one call site. A single ?.let is cheaper than a class.
  • Value types. Zero, empty string, empty list already work.
Situation Better choice
Optional dependency (logger, analytics) Null Object
Lookup may fail, caller should handle Optional / nullable / sealed result
Collection absent empty collection
Absence is an error throw / fail fast

Android angle. Analytics: AnalyticsTracker interface with FirebaseTracker and NoOpTracker for debug and unit tests; the DI module (Hilt) binds the right one per build type. This is a clean, common senior answer.

Everyday analogy. A dummy plug in an unused socket: safe to touch, does nothing, saves checking if the hole is empty.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing Null Object to hide the fact that required data is missing.
  • Not mentioning Optional or Kotlin nullable types as alternatives.

notes.title: Specification: the idea
notes.html:
Specification wraps a business rule in an object with a method like isSatisfiedBy(candidate), and lets you combine rules with AND, OR and NOT. Instead of building long conditions with flags, you compose small, named, testable rules.

Use it for dynamic filtering, validation and eligibility: "premium user AND account older than 30 days AND NOT blocked".

+-------------------+
| <<interface>>     |
| Spec<T>           |  isSatisfiedBy(t): bool
| and(), or(), not()|
+--------+----------+
         ^
 +-------+---------+------------+
 |       |         |            |
Leaf   AndSpec   OrSpec     NotSpec    (composite)
specs

Before: a query method with many boolean parameters.

List<User> find(boolean premium, boolean oldAccount, boolean notBlocked, String city) {
    List<User> r = new ArrayList<>();
    for (User u : all) {
        if (premium && !u.isPremium()) continue;
        if (oldAccount && u.ageDays() < 30) continue;
        if (notBlocked && u.isBlocked()) continue;
        if (city != null && !city.equals(u.city())) continue;
        r.add(u);
    }
    return r;
}

Every new filter changes the signature of every caller (combinatorial explosion).

After:

@FunctionalInterface
interface Spec<T> {
    boolean isSatisfiedBy(T t);
    default Spec<T> and(Spec<T> o) { return t -> isSatisfiedBy(t) && o.isSatisfiedBy(t); }
    default Spec<T> or(Spec<T> o)  { return t -> isSatisfiedBy(t) || o.isSatisfiedBy(t); }
    default Spec<T> not()          { return t -> !isSatisfiedBy(t); }
}

Spec<User> premium   = User::isPremium;
Spec<User> oldAcct   = u -> u.ageDays() >= 30;
Spec<User> blocked   = User::isBlocked;
Spec<User> eligible  = premium.and(oldAcct).and(blocked.not());

all.stream().filter(eligible::isSatisfiedBy).toList();

Each rule has one name, one test, and can be reused for validation ("is this user eligible?"), selection ("find all eligible users") and construction ("create an eligible user").

Kotlin variant. Function types and extension functions do it concisely:

typealias Spec<T> = (T) -> Boolean
infix fun <T> Spec<T>.and(o: Spec<T>): Spec<T> = { this(it) && o(it) }
infix fun <T> Spec<T>.or(o: Spec<T>): Spec<T> = { this(it) || o(it) }
operator fun <T> Spec<T>.not(): Spec<T> = { !this(it) }

val premium: Spec<User> = { it.isPremium }
val old: Spec<User> = { it.ageDays >= 30 }
val blocked: Spec<User> = { it.isBlocked }
val eligible = premium and old and !blocked
users.filter(eligible)

Real examples. Spring Data JPA Specification<T> (Specification.where(a).and(b), translated to SQL WHERE), JPA Criteria API, Hibernate filters, Guava Predicate and Java java.util.function.Predicate (the and/or/negate methods are exactly this), Room dynamic queries via SupportSQLiteQuery, ElasticSearch bool queries, feature-flag targeting rules.

Worked example. A search screen has 8 optional filters. Booleans give 2^8 = 256 combinations in one method. With specs, you add each active filter to a list and reduce(Spec::and): 8 small classes/lambdas, each tested once. With JPA specs, and becomes a SQL AND, so filtering runs in the database (10 ms for an indexed query) instead of loading 1,000,000 rows into memory (several seconds, about 500 MB).

When NOT to use Specification.

  • Two or three fixed conditions: write the if.
  • A single place uses the rule: a lambda inline is enough.
  • Performance: if rules are in-memory predicates over huge data, push them to the database (query specs), do not stream everything.
  • Using Predicate from the standard library already covers it; build a custom Spec only for domain naming or SQL translation.

Decision gravity. Cheap and reversible in memory. When specs are translated to SQL, the spec language becomes coupled to your schema: renaming a column breaks specs at runtime, not compile time (use the JPA metamodel or typed queries like jOOQ, Room, SQLDelight).

Everyday analogy. Filter chips on a shopping site: "under 5000", "4 stars+", "in stock"; each is a rule, and you stack them.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Specification is the same as Strategy: a spec answers yes/no about a candidate and combines; a strategy computes something.
  • In-memory filtering of a huge dataset where the DB should filter.
  • Specs with side effects; they must be pure.

notes.title: Behavioral patterns compared: how to choose
notes.html:
Most behavioral patterns look alike on a class diagram (an interface plus implementations). The difference is the intent and who is in control. Ask: what changes, what triggers it, and who decides?

Pattern Core question it answers Who decides / triggers Typical sign you need it
Strategy Which algorithm to use? client picks big if/else choosing a method
Template Method Fixed steps, variable details? base class drives copy-pasted skeleton, small differences
Observer Who gets told when X changes? subject pushes polling, hard-coded callbacks
Mediator How do many objects coordinate? the hub decides N objects calling each other
State Behaviour per mode? the object moves itself if (state == ...) in every method
Command How do I treat a request as data? invoker runs it later queue, undo, log, retry
Chain of Responsibility Who handles this request? each handler passes or stops ordered checks, middleware
Iterator How to walk without knowing structure? client pulls loops differ per container
Memento How to save and restore state? caretaker holds undo, checkpoints
Visitor Add operations without editing classes? operation moves to visitor many instanceof checks, stable types
Interpreter Evaluate a small language? parser builds tree rules/expressions as text
Null Object What if there is nothing? default object if (x != null) everywhere
Specification Can I combine business rules? rules composed boolean-flag filters

The look-alike pairs interviewers ask about.

  • Strategy vs State: same shape. Strategy: client chooses and rarely changes it; states transition themselves and know each other.
  • Strategy vs Template Method: composition at runtime vs inheritance at compile time.
  • Command vs Strategy: a Command is a request (receiver + args + maybe undo); a Strategy is an algorithm.
  • Observer vs Mediator: broadcast with no logic vs central coordination with logic.
  • Observer vs Pub/Sub: direct references vs a broker between them.
  • Chain vs Decorator: a chain handler may stop the request; a decorator always forwards and augments.
  • Visitor vs Interpreter: Visitor adds operations to a structure; Interpreter evaluates a grammar tree (and may use Visitor).
  • Memento vs Command-undo: snapshot vs inverse operation.

Everyday analogy. Same wheels, different vehicles: all behavioral patterns use polymorphism, yet a bus, a taxi and a train each answer a different transport question.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming a pattern before describing the problem. Start with "the pain is...".
  • Memorising definitions without naming the cost.

notes.title: Choosing in practice: three worked scenarios
notes.html:
Scenario 1: Checkout with promo codes, payment methods and order status.

  • Promo calculation varies by code type -> Strategy (or Specification for eligibility).
  • Payment steps (authorise, capture, notify) identical across gateways except API calls -> Template Method or Strategy per gateway.
  • Order lifecycle (Created, Paid, Shipped, Delivered) -> State / FSM with a transition table and DB guard.
  • Notifications on state change -> Observer / domain events; to other services -> pub/sub (Kafka).
  • Undo of cart edits -> Command with a history stack.

Scenario 2: Android feed screen.

  • UI state flows ViewModel -> UI -> Observer (StateFlow) ; one-off navigation -> SharedFlow/channel.
  • Network layer logging, auth, retries -> Chain of Responsibility (OkHttp interceptors).
  • Pagination -> Iterator-like (Paging 3).
  • Analytics optional in debug -> Null Object.
  • Filtering posts by user-chosen chips -> Specification.
  • Save scroll and form state across process death -> Memento (SavedStateHandle).

Scenario 3: In-app rules engine.

  • Rule text age > 18 AND country = IN -> Interpreter (small grammar) with sealed classes.
  • Operations on the rule tree (evaluate, pretty print, optimise) -> Visitor / sealed when.
  • Composing programmatic rules -> Specification.

Worked sizing. For 3 promo types, an if is fine (about 20 lines). At 12 promo types with unit tests per type, Strategy pays for itself: 12 small classes, each tested alone. The break-even is about 4 to 5 variants or when variants appear regularly.

Decision gravity. Pick the lightest mechanism that handles current variants: function, enum, then pattern. Moving up (enum -> Strategy) is a cheap refactor; moving down (removing a pattern used everywhere) is expensive because call sites depend on the indirection. Over-engineering, not under-engineering, is the more common interview failure.

Everyday analogy. Kitchen tools: you do not use a food processor to slice one tomato.

Common interview traps.

  • Listing every pattern in the solution. Use two or three that match real pain.
  • Ignoring simpler language features: lambdas, enums with behaviour, sealed classes, extension functions.
  • Not mentioning testing benefits (inject a fake strategy, a no-op logger, a recorded event stream).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Null Object: a harmless default implementation replacing null (NoOpLogger, emptyList()); use when doing nothing is correct, not to hide missing required dependencies. Alternatives: Optional, nullable types, sealed Result, fail fast.
  • Specification: named, composable yes/no rules (and, or, not) used for validation, selection and construction; Spring Data JPA Specification and java.util.function.Predicate are examples. Push heavy filtering to the database.
  • Choosing: ask what varies and who triggers it. Algorithm choice -> Strategy; fixed skeleton -> Template; notification -> Observer; coordination hub -> Mediator; per-mode behaviour -> State; request as data/undo -> Command; handler pipeline -> Chain; traversal -> Iterator; snapshot -> Memento; new operations on stable types -> Visitor; small grammar -> Interpreter.
  • Know the look-alike pairs (Strategy/State, Observer/Mediator, Command/Strategy, Chain/Decorator) and answer with intent, not shape.
  • Prefer the lightest tool first (lambda, enum, sealed class); a pattern is worth it at roughly 4 or more real variants or when testing/undo/queuing needs it.
  • In interviews: describe the pain, show before and after, state the cost and when not to use it.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Null Object pattern, and how does it differ from returning null or Optional?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can pick the right "nothing": a harmless default, a forced decision, or a failure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Null Object is a do-nothing implementation of an interface that I hand out instead of null. The caller just calls the method and the null object does a harmless default, so there are no if (x != null) checks to forget. I use it when doing nothing is the correct behaviour, like an optional logger or analytics tracker. If absence is meaningful and the caller must react, I use Optional, a nullable type or a sealed result; if it is a bug, I fail fast.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client -> Logger interface -> ConsoleLogger
                           -> NoOpLogger   (null object)

One shared immutable instance is enough (a singleton). Standard library cousins: Collections.emptyList(), SLF4J NOPLogger, Optional.empty() (a value wrapper, not a behaviour).

Situation Better choice
Optional dependency (logger, analytics) Null Object
Lookup may fail, caller handles it Optional / nullable / sealed result
Collection absent empty collection
Absence is an error throw / fail fast

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

interface Logger { void log(String msg); }
class NoOpLogger implements Logger { public void log(String m) { } }
class Service {
    private final Logger logger;
    Service(Logger logger) { this.logger = logger; }   // never null
    void run() { logger.log("start"); doWork(); logger.log("end"); }
}
interface Logger { fun log(msg: String) }
object NoOpLogger : Logger { override fun log(msg: String) {} }
class Service(private val logger: Logger = NoOpLogger) {
    fun run() { logger.log("start") }
}
fun loadTags(): List<String> = emptyList()   // value case: empty, not null

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it where failure should be loud (payments, security).
  • Returning null for a collection instead of empty.
  • Allocating a new null object each time instead of one shared instance.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does Kotlin need it? -> Less for values (?., ?:), still useful for behaviour defaults.
  2. Null Object vs Optional? -> Behaviour default vs value wrapper that forces the caller to decide.
  3. What is the hidden risk? -> It hides a missing dependency; a silent success can be worse than an NPE.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "avoid null checks". Senior chooses among Null Object, Optional and fail-fast by what absence means.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 13th call site forgot a logger != null check, causing an NPE only when logging was disabled, a rare config found after release.

questions.contextHtml:
In a code review you see this change meant to "fix a crash in the test environment":

class NullPaymentGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public PaymentResult charge(Order o) { return PaymentResult.success("n/a"); }
}
@Bean PaymentGateway gateway(@Value("${pay.url:}") String url) {
    return url.isBlank() ? new NullPaymentGateway() : new HttpPaymentGateway(url);
}

Two weeks later finance reports 214 orders marked "paid" with no money collected; a deploy lost the pay.url environment variable.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong with the pattern choice, and what should the code do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a log line" or "set the variable"; keeps the null object.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a blank URL ever valid in production? How were orders fulfilled? Is there reconciliation?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop fulfilment for affected orders; fix config; reconcile with the gateway's records.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Null Object used for a required dependency; config failure silently degrades; no startup validation.
  4. How I'd verify each: Query orders by payment id "n/a"; diff deploy env; check startup logs.
  5. Root cause: Doing nothing is not a correct payment behaviour, so "success" is a lie; a null object turned a config error into data corruption.
  6. Fix: Fail fast at startup:
@Bean PaymentGateway gateway(@Value("${pay.url}") String url) {
    if (url.isBlank()) throw new IllegalStateException("pay.url is required");
    return new HttpPaymentGateway(url);
}

Tests use an explicit FakePaymentGateway (recording, can fail) via a test profile, not a production fallback. 7. Prevention: Required-config validation at boot; reconciliation job; alert on payment id "n/a". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep a Null Object even if it returns "failure": the caller then must handle it, which is Optional/result semantics, not a harmless default.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Optional analytics tracker, same approach? -> Yes: there, doing nothing is correct.
  • Sandbox mode wanted? -> A named SandboxGateway enabled by an explicit flag, visible in logs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "convenient" no-op payment fallback marked hundreds of orders as paid; the fix was a one-line startup failure and a reconciliation job.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds logging.
  • Hire: removes the null object for a required dependency.
  • Strong hire: fail-fast config, explicit fakes in tests, reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml: An Android app calls analytics?.track("checkout_started") in 60 places; in 7 of them a developer forgot ?. after making analytics nullable in a refactor and used !!, giving crashes in debug builds where analytics is disabled. Unit tests need to assert which events fired. Release uses Firebase.
questions.promptHtml: How would you restructure analytics so call sites are clean, debug builds are safe and tests can verify events?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: More ?. and a global if (BuildConfig.DEBUG).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a DI framework (Hilt)? Are events fire-and-forget? Any privacy gates (consent)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace !! with a default instance.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Nullable dependency is the smell; an interface with a no-op implementation removes the branch.
  4. How I'd verify each: Grep analytics!! and ?.track; run the debug build.
  5. Root cause: Optional collaborator modeled as null.
  6. Fix:
interface AnalyticsTracker { fun track(event: String, props: Map<String, Any> = emptyMap()) }
object NoOpTracker : AnalyticsTracker { override fun track(event: String, props: Map<String, Any>) {} }
class FirebaseTracker(private val fa: FirebaseAnalytics) : AnalyticsTracker { /* ... */ }
class RecordingTracker : AnalyticsTracker { val events = mutableListOf<String>(); override fun track(event: String, props: Map<String, Any>) { events += event } }
// Hilt: bind FirebaseTracker in release, NoOpTracker in debug, RecordingTracker in tests
interface AnalyticsTracker { void track(String event); }
enum NoOpTracker implements AnalyticsTracker { INSTANCE; public void track(String e) { } }
  1. Prevention: Constructor injection (non-null); a unit test with RecordingTracker asserting events.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make a global singleton tracker; injection keeps tests isolated. And I would not no-op consent-required tracking silently without documenting it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• User revokes consent at runtime? -> Swap to a no-op through a delegating tracker that checks a consent flag.
  • Is Null Object overkill for one call site? -> Yes; a ?.let is cheaper.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single forgotten null check crashed only in debug builds; a no-op tracker removed the whole class of bugs and made event tests trivial.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more null checks.
  • Hire: NoOp via DI.
  • Strong hire: recording fake for tests, consent handling, and when it is overkill.

questions.contextHtml: A review comment says "use Null Object everywhere to avoid nulls". Three places in the codebase: (1) findUser(id) returns null when not found and the controller returns 404; (2) getDiscount(user) returns null when there is no discount, callers then if (d != null) total -= d.amount; (3) getReviews(productId) returns null if none exist, three callers crash on .size().
questions.promptHtml: For each, what do you return and why? Where would Null Object be wrong?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Applies Null Object to all three, or says "just use Optional" for all.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: In (1) must the caller react differently? In (2) is "no discount" a normal business state? In (3) any semantic difference between none and unknown?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the crash in (3) by returning an empty list.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) caller must decide: absence is meaningful. (2) no discount is a legit rule: Null Object fits. (3) empty collection is the null object for collections.
  4. How I'd verify each: Walk callers; check each branch's behaviour on absence.
  5. Root cause: Using null for three different meanings.
  6. Fix:
fun findUser(id: Id): User?                      // forces the caller to handle 404
interface Discount { fun apply(total: Money): Money }
object NoDiscount : Discount { override fun apply(total: Money) = total }
fun getDiscount(u: User): Discount = ...         // never null
fun getReviews(pid: Id): List<Review> = emptyList()
Optional<User> findUser(Id id);
Discount getDiscount(User u);   // returns NoDiscount.INSTANCE
List<Review> getReviews(Id pid); // List.of() when none
  1. Prevention: Static nullability annotations or Kotlin types; a style rule "no null collections".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a NullUser for (1): returning a fake user lets deleted users log in or hides a 404.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• NoDiscount needs to appear in the UI? -> Then absence is meaningful for display: model Optional/nullable and show nothing.
  • Is Optional for fields good? -> Prefer it for return types, not fields or parameters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A NullUser fallback let deleted accounts pass a permission check for a week; the fix was a nullable return the caller had to handle.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one tool for all.
  • Hire: maps each case correctly.
  • Strong hire: explains the intent of "nothing" per case and names the NullUser danger.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Specification pattern, and how is it different from Strategy and from Predicate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you see composable business rules, and can tell look-alikes apart.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Specification wraps a business rule in an object with isSatisfiedBy(candidate) and lets me combine rules with AND, OR and NOT. Instead of long conditions with flags, I compose small named rules that are individually testable and reusable for validation, selection and construction. It differs from Strategy because a spec answers yes or no about a candidate and combines, while a strategy computes something. java.util.function.Predicate already gives and/or/negate; I add a custom Spec for domain naming or SQL translation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Premium rule -> AND -> Old account rule -> AND -> NOT blocked -> Eligible

It is a Composite: leaf specs plus And/Or/Not. Spring Data JPA Specification<T> is the database version: and becomes a SQL AND, so the filtering runs in the database instead of in memory. Specs must be pure (no side effects).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

@FunctionalInterface
interface Spec<T> {
    boolean isSatisfiedBy(T t);
    default Spec<T> and(Spec<T> o) { return t -> isSatisfiedBy(t) && o.isSatisfiedBy(t); }
    default Spec<T> or(Spec<T> o)  { return t -> isSatisfiedBy(t) || o.isSatisfiedBy(t); }
    default Spec<T> not()          { return t -> !isSatisfiedBy(t); }
}
Spec<User> eligible = ((Spec<User>) User::isPremium).and(u -> u.ageDays() >= 30).and(((Spec<User>) User::isBlocked).not());
typealias Spec<T> = (T) -> Boolean
infix fun <T> Spec<T>.and(o: Spec<T>): Spec<T> = { this(it) && o(it) }
operator fun <T> Spec<T>.not(): Spec<T> = { !this(it) }
val premium: Spec<User> = { it.isPremium }
val blocked: Spec<User> = { it.isBlocked }
val eligible = premium and !blocked

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying Specification equals Strategy.
  • Loading a million rows to filter in memory when the DB should filter.
  • Specs with side effects.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not booleans parameters? -> 8 optional filters give 256 combinations in one signature; specs compose.
  2. Where does it go wrong? -> Rules coupled to column names via strings: renames break at runtime, so use typed metamodels.
  3. Is a custom Spec class needed over Predicate? -> Only for domain naming, explanations ("why did it fail?") or query translation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE shows and/or. Senior ties it to validation/selection/construction, pushes it to SQL, and keeps specs pure.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A search screen with 8 optional filters went from a 300-line method to 8 specs; JPA specs moved filtering into the DB (10 ms vs seconds).

questions.contextHtml: A UserRepository.find(boolean premium, boolean oldAccount, boolean notBlocked, String city, Integer minAge, ...) has 8 parameters; callers pass null/false for most. A 9th filter "has verified email" arrives; 14 callers use positional arguments and two tests broke after the last addition. The query is in memory over all (about 200,000 users).
questions.promptHtml: Refactor it. What classes appear, and what happens when the next filter arrives?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds a 9th parameter or a builder with the same if-chain inside.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are filters always ANDed or sometimes OR/NOT? Is data in a DB? Do filters also validate single users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Introduce Predicate<User> composition without changing callers yet.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Combinatorial explosion; the same rules reused for validation; in-memory scan of 200,000 rows per call.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count call patterns; time the in-memory filter.
  5. Root cause: Rules embedded as flags in one method.
  6. Fix:
Spec<User> premium = User::isPremium;
Spec<User> verified = User::isEmailVerified;           // 9th filter: one line
Spec<User> active = notBlocked.and(oldAcct);
List<Spec<User>> chosen = filtersFromRequest(req);
Spec<User> all = chosen.stream().reduce(u -> true, Spec::and);
repo.find(all);
val spec = filters.fold<Spec<User>, Spec<User>>({ true }) { acc, s -> acc and s }
users.filter(spec)

In the DB version, repo.findAll(Specification.where(a).and(b)). 7. Prevention: Each spec has a tiny unit test; reuse the spec for isEligible(user) validation. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use a custom Spec if only two fixed conditions exist; an if is clearer. Specs for in-memory scans of 200,000 rows should move to SQL.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need "why was this user excluded"? -> Specs return a result with a reason, or compose named specs and report the first failing one.
  • OR across filters from UI chips? -> Group by category: OR within a category, AND across.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A filter method with 11 parameters took three bugs a month; turning each into a spec dropped it to zero in six months.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: 9th parameter.
  • Hire: Spec composition.
  • Strong hire: reuse for validation, DB translation and a note on when not to use it.

questions.contextHtml:
An admin search uses in-memory Spec<Order> composition over orderRepo.findAll(). Table: 1,000,000 orders, about 500 B each.

heap used (admin pod)  3.2 GB of 4 GB    GC pause p99 1.8 s
search latency p50     6.5 s
db rows scanned        1,000,000 per search
searches per minute    40

A teammate proposes "cache all orders in memory"; another proposes more pods.
questions.promptHtml: Fix it while keeping the benefits of composable rules.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Caching everything or scaling pods; keeps filtering in Java.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which filters are indexed? Freshness needs? Are rules purely column-based or do some need domain logic?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a mandatory date range and a limit.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Filtering in Java after loading the table; missing indexes; GC from huge lists.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN of the query; heap histogram; count rows returned vs scanned.
  5. Root cause: Specs evaluated as in-memory predicates instead of being translated into the query.
  6. Fix: Use query specs that translate to SQL:
Specification<Order> spec = Specification.where(statusIs(PAID)).and(createdAfter(from)).and(cityIn(cities));
Page<Order> page = repo.findAll(spec, PageRequest.of(0, 50, Sort.by("createdAt").descending()));

Add composite indexes for the common combos. Keep an in-memory Spec only for rules that cannot be expressed in SQL, applied to the small page afterwards. 7. Prevention: A guard that rejects unpaginated queries; slow-query alerting; typed metamodel (Order_.status) so renames fail at compile time. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cache a million orders per pod (stale, memory-bound). Spec language coupled to the schema is the price; metamodel or jOOQ/Room-typed queries reduce the risk.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A filter needs a Java-only rule? -> SQL first, then in-memory spec on the narrowed set.
  • Many OR branches hurting the plan? -> Check the plan; consider UNION or search engine.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Moving the same composed rules from memory to SQL reduced a 6 s search to 40 ms with an index; the rules and tests stayed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cache or scale.
  • Hire: pushes filtering to DB with JPA specifications.
  • Strong hire: indexes, pagination guard, typed metamodel and hybrid fallback.

questions.promptHtml: Behavioral patterns look the same on a class diagram. How do you tell Strategy from State, Observer from Mediator, and Chain from Decorator?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests intent over shape, the most common senior-level pattern question.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The shape is an interface plus implementations; the difference is who decides and what changes. Strategy: the client picks an algorithm and rarely swaps it. State: the object moves itself between states, and states know each other. Observer: the subject broadcasts with no logic; Mediator: a hub coordinates with logic. Chain: a handler may stop the request; Decorator always forwards and augments.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Pair Difference
Strategy vs State client-chosen algorithm vs self-driven transitions
Strategy vs Template Method runtime composition vs compile-time inheritance
Command vs Strategy a request (receiver, args, undo) vs an algorithm
Observer vs Mediator broadcast vs central coordination logic
Observer vs Pub/Sub direct references vs a broker
Chain vs Decorator may stop vs always forwards
Visitor vs Interpreter add operations to a structure vs evaluate a grammar tree
Memento vs Command-undo snapshot vs inverse operation

I start the answer with the pain ("N objects call each other"), not the pattern name.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

// Strategy: caller chooses. State: object moves itself.
interface Discount { double apply(double t); }          // Strategy
interface OrderState { OrderState next(Event e); }      // State: returns the next state
fun interface Discount { fun apply(t: Double): Double }          // Strategy
sealed interface OrderState { fun next(e: Event): OrderState }   // State transitions itself

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Naming a pattern before describing the pain.
  • Memorising definitions without naming the cost.
  • Calling a lambda "Strategy pattern" and stopping there.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Strategy vs lambda? -> A lambda is the lightest Strategy; make a class when it has state, a name and tests.
  2. Observer vs Pub/Sub? -> Observer holds direct references in one process; pub/sub adds a broker, async delivery, decoupled lifecycles.
  3. Can a Chain contain Strategies? -> Yes; each handler can delegate to a strategy for its decision.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "Strategy is for algorithms". Senior answers by trigger and control, and names the cost.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team labelled a state machine "Strategy" and allowed external code to swap states; invalid transitions reached production.

questions.contextHtml:
A developer modeled an order lifecycle as "Strategy":

class Order {
    private OrderBehavior behavior = new CreatedBehavior();
    void setBehavior(OrderBehavior b) { this.behavior = b; }     // public
    void ship() { behavior.ship(this); }
}
// Somewhere in a controller:
order.setBehavior(new DeliveredBehavior());
order.ship();     // allowed? ships a delivered order

Incident: 17 orders shipped twice after a retry path called setBehavior directly. Metrics: duplicate shipments 0.4% of orders; no exceptions logged.
questions.promptHtml: Name the right pattern, fix the code, and explain the difference.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an if check in ship."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which transitions are legal? Does persistence also store the state? Are there concurrent writers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make setBehavior private and add a DB guard (UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'PAID').
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Wrong pattern (a lifecycle is State); public setter lets outsiders force a state; no idempotency on the retry path.
  4. How I'd verify each: Search for external setBehavior calls; replay the retry path in a test.
  5. Root cause: Strategy lets the client choose and swap; the lifecycle needs the object (or its states) to own transitions.
  6. Fix:
sealed interface OrderState permits Created, Paid, Shipped, Delivered {
    default OrderState ship() { throw new IllegalStateException("cannot ship from " + this); }
}
final class Paid implements OrderState { public OrderState ship() { return new Shipped(); } }
class Order {
    private OrderState state = new Created();
    void ship() { state = state.ship(); }    // states decide the next state
}
sealed interface OrderState {
    fun ship(): OrderState = error("cannot ship from $this")
    object Paid : OrderState { override fun ship() = Shipped }
    object Shipped : OrderState
}

Persist the state and update with a conditional write for concurrency. 7. Prevention: Transition table tests (all legal and illegal pairs); idempotency key on the retry path. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use State for a two-status flag (an enum is enough). I would not rely on in-memory guards alone: two servers need a DB-level check.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same shape as Strategy, so why does it matter? -> Control and invariants: States enforce legal moves; strategies are interchangeable.
  • Concurrent ship requests? -> Optimistic lock or conditional update.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Duplicate shipments came from a public setter on a "strategy"; making transitions private removed them without touching the retry logic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds an if.
  • Hire: State with private transitions.
  • Strong hire: DB-level guard, idempotency and transition-table tests.

questions.contextHtml: Design the behavioral side of a checkout: 3 promo types today (percentage, flat, buy-one-get-one) with 12 expected in a year; 2 payment gateways with identical authorise-capture-notify steps but different API calls; order lifecycle Created, Paid, Shipped, Delivered, Cancelled; email and analytics on every state change; cart edits with undo. Time: 4 weeks, 3 engineers. An architect says "use all the GoF patterns for future-proofing".
questions.promptHtml: Which patterns do you pick for which part, and what do you deliberately NOT build yet?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Names every pattern, or none.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How fast do promo types grow? Are gateways added by us or partners? Are state changes consumed by other services? Is undo local to the client?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design); I would decide by pain per part.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Promo calc: if at 3 types, Strategy at about 4+ or when unit tests per type are wanted; Specification for eligibility rules. Payment: Template Method or one Strategy per gateway. Lifecycle: State with a transition table plus a DB guard. State-change effects: Observer in process, domain events and pub/sub across services. Undo: Command with a history stack.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count variants and change frequency in the backlog; check who consumes events.
  5. Root cause: Over- or under-engineering from picking by name, not by pain.
  6. Fix:
Promo (Strategy + Spec) -> Payment (Template/Strategy) -> Order (State) -> Events (Observer) -> Email/Analytics
Cart edits -> Command + undo stack

Build now: State for the order, Strategy as a fun interface for promos, Observer for events. Defer: Visitor, Interpreter, Mediator. 7. Prevention: Tests inject a fake strategy, a no-op notifier and a recording event stream. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build an Interpreter promo-rules DSL or a plugin framework in four weeks; the lightest mechanism that handles current variants wins, and moving up (enum to Strategy) is a cheap refactor while removing a deep pattern is not.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Promos hit 12 types with partner-defined rules? -> Then Specification plus data-driven rules, maybe a small Interpreter.
  • Payment steps differ per gateway? -> Switch from Template Method to Strategy per gateway.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch carried 9 patterns for 3 variants; a year later two were still unused and the team deleted them at cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lists all patterns.
  • Hire: maps pain to pattern for each part.
  • Strong hire: sizing thresholds, explicit deferrals and testability.

questions.contextHtml: You are reviewing an Android feed screen design doc. It proposes: a Mediator class coordinating network, DB, UI and analytics; a Visitor over Post types (text, image, video: stable for 2 years); Memento in a custom class for scroll position; a hand-written iterator for pagination; a custom LogSpec and analytics with if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) checks. App must survive rotation and process death, retry failed calls with auth, and let users filter by chips.
questions.promptHtml: Which proposals do you accept, replace or reject, and with what platform-native mechanisms?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts all as written, or rejects everything as over-engineering.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Post hierarchy closed? How many chips? Offline needed? Existing Hilt/Paging/Room?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design review).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: UI state flows from ViewModel via StateFlow (Observer), not a Mediator class. Pagination is Paging 3. Scroll and form state: SavedStateHandle/rememberSaveable (Memento). Network concerns: OkHttp interceptors (Chain). Optional analytics: Null Object via DI. Chip filters: Specification (or a Room query). Post rendering: sealed when instead of Visitor.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype rotate and process-death tests; check library availability.
  5. Root cause: Reinventing framework features and choosing Visitor despite a closed type set with only one operation (render).
  6. Fix:
sealed interface Post { data class Text(...) : Post; data class Image(...) : Post; data class Video(...) : Post }
@Composable fun PostItem(p: Post) = when (p) { is Post.Text -> TextRow(p); is Post.Image -> ImageRow(p); is Post.Video -> VideoRow(p) }
class FeedVm(handle: SavedStateHandle, repo: FeedRepo, tracker: AnalyticsTracker) : ViewModel() {
    val state: StateFlow<FeedState> = ...
    val feed = Pager(PagingConfig(20)) { repo.pagingSource(filter) }.flow.cachedIn(viewModelScope)
}
  1. Prevention: Tests with fake repo, NoOpTracker/RecordingTracker; rotation and process-death instrumentation test.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not write a hand-rolled iterator for paging, nor a Visitor for one operation over a stable sealed type. I would accept Specification only if filters combine freely; otherwise a Room query with parameters.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not Mediator? -> The ViewModel is already the coordination point; a separate god class adds indirection.
  • A fourth post type arrives? -> Compiler errors at the when, easy to find.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A design doc with six patterns became four framework features and one sealed when; code volume dropped by half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts everything or rejects with no alternative.
  • Hire: maps to framework features.
  • Strong hire: explains each replacement, tests (rotation, process death) and when custom patterns would be justified.

questions.promptHtml: How do you decide whether a problem deserves a design pattern at all, or just a function, an enum or a sealed class?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Over-engineering is the most common senior-level failure; this checks judgement and the reversibility argument.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I pick the lightest mechanism that handles the current variants: a function, then an enum with behaviour, then a sealed class, then a pattern. Strategy usually pays off at about 4 to 5 real variants, or sooner when I need per-variant tests, undo or queuing. Moving up (enum to Strategy) is a cheap refactor; removing a pattern that call sites depend on is expensive, so under-building first is the safer error.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Known key -> Map lookup | Ordered cross-cutting steps -> Chain | Notify everyone -> Observer

Worked sizing: 3 promo types is about 20 lines of if; at 12 types with unit tests per type, 12 small Strategy classes each tested alone win. Language features cover many patterns: lambdas (Strategy, Command), Predicate (Specification), sealed when (Visitor), emptyList() (Null Object), sequence {} (Iterator). I begin with the pain, show before and after, then state the cost and when not to use it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

enum Promo {                                   // enough for 3 stable variants
    PERCENT { double apply(double t) { return t * 0.9; } },
    FLAT    { double apply(double t) { return t - 50; } };
    abstract double apply(double t);
}
fun interface PromoStrategy { fun apply(total: Double): Double }
val promos = mapOf("PERCENT" to PromoStrategy { it * 0.9 }, "FLAT" to PromoStrategy { it - 50 })

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Listing every pattern in one solution; use two or three that match real pain.
  • Ignoring lambdas, enums with behaviour, sealed classes and extension functions.
  • Not mentioning testing benefits (fake strategy, no-op logger, recorded events).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is an enum not enough? -> When variants need injected dependencies, state or are added by other modules.
  2. How do you justify a pattern in review? -> Name the pain, show the diff, state the cost and the trigger for removing it.
  3. Which direction of refactor is cheaper? -> Up the ladder; call sites then depend on a small interface.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE reaches for GoF names. Senior reaches for the language first, quantifies the break-even and treats patterns as reversible tools.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A one-time promo if was replaced by a Strategy framework with 3 implementations and a registry; two years later it still had 3.
